question: What are the three parts of the epidemiological triad used to study how diseases spread?
explanation: Think of the triad as a stool with three legs: the infectious agent, the susceptible host, and the environment. All three must interact for an infection to take root! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h1)

question: Why is a host so important in the disease transmission cycle?

options.A: Because pathogens can survive and multiply indefinitely without any living host
options.B: Because the host creates the original genetic makeup of the pathogen
options.C: Because the host destroys all environmental factors immediately
options.D: Because an infectious agent needs a living organism to harbor it and cause infection

explanation: Pathogens need a home to thrive! Just like a guest needs a house, an infectious agent needs a living host to set up camp and multiply. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h1)

question: What do we call a host where a parasite or pathogen grows up and reproduces?

options.A: An organism where the infectious agent reaches maturity and reproduces
options.B: An organism that can catch an infection but never pass it on
options.C: An environmental source where bacteria live without growing
options.D: An insect that only carries a virus on its outer legs

explanation: This is known as the definitive host. It's the place where the pathogen finally grows into its adult, reproductive stage. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h2)

question: What makes a host a 'dead-end host' during an infection?

options.A: The host destroys the infectious agent completely upon first contact
options.B: The host harbors the adult parasite for many years without harm
options.C: The host cannot pass the infection on to other susceptible individuals
options.D: The host dies immediately before any symptoms can manifest

explanation: Think of it as a dead-end street. The pathogen gets stuck inside this host and cannot travel any further to infect other people. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h2)

question: In public health, what does 'host resistance' mean?

options.A: The physical barrier created by wearing heavy protective clothing
options.B: The ability of an infectious agent to survive inside a harsh environment
options.C: The total of all natural and acquired defenses that protect against infection
options.D: The rate at which a community spreads a contagious virus

explanation: Host resistance is your body's shield—all your natural and built-up defenses working together to keep germs out and stop infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h3)

question: A poorly nourished child living in a crowded area comes down with frequent infections. Which factor is most responsible for lowering this child's defenses?

options.A: An advanced age causing a natural decline in immunity
options.B: A high level of physical fitness preventing disease spread
options.C: Inherited genetic immunity protecting against parasites
options.D: Compromised nutritional status weakening immune defenses

explanation: Good nutrition is fuel for the immune system. When a child lacks proper nutrients, their body simply doesn't have the strength to fight off everyday germs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h3)

question: What is an asymptomatic carrier?

options.A: A host who harbors an infectious agent without showing illness but can still spread it
options.B: A patient who has completely recovered and has lifelong immunity to a virus
options.C: An environmental surface that holds bacteria without allowing them to multiply
options.D: An animal that serves as the final dead-end host for a dangerous parasite

explanation: An asymptomatic carrier feels totally fine and shows no signs of sickness, but they are secretly carrying and spreading the germ to others. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h4)

question: Why are asymptomatic carriers so tricky to deal with during disease outbreaks?

options.A: They develop severe complications that require immediate intensive care unit admission
options.B: They continue normal daily activities and spread the pathogen without knowing they are sick
options.C: They destroy the infection too quickly for laboratory tests to detect any antibodies
options.D: They carry mutated strains of bacteria that are completely immune to all known antibiotics

explanation: Because they don't feel sick, they don't stay home or isolate. They walk around living life normally while unintentionally passing the virus or bacteria along. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h4)

question: How does a person's body build active immunity?

options.A: Through passive transfer of maternal antibodies across the placenta
options.B: Through genetic traits inherited directly from parents at birth
options.C: Through receiving temporary antibodies directly from an animal serum injection
options.D: Through the host's own immune system producing antibodies after exposure to a pathogen or vaccine

explanation: Active immunity means your body does the heavy lifting! Your own immune cells fight the germ (or vaccine) and remember it for the future. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h5)

question: What is the main superpower of herd immunity in a community?

options.A: It ensures that all infectious agents mutate into harmless forms of microbes
options.B: It guarantees that every single person in the population will never get infected
options.C: It protects vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated by breaking the transmission chain
options.D: It eliminates all environmental sources of bacteria within a specific geographical area

explanation: When almost everyone around is immune, the germ has nowhere to jump. This creates a protective shield around babies or sick folks who can't take vaccines. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT something a nurse checks when assessing a patient's personal host status?

options.A: Screening for underlying chronic illnesses like diabetes
options.B: Inquiring about recent travel history to endemic regions
options.C: Reviewing the patient's personal immunization records
options.D: Analyzing the genetic makeup of the local water supply

explanation: Host assessment is all about the *person* sitting in front of you—their health, vaccines, and history. Water genetics belong to environmental health, not individual patient assessment! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h6)

question: A nurse is caring for an adult with diabetes who works on a farm. What is the most important health risk to keep an eye on?

options.A: Absence of any need for routine immunization boosters
options.C: Increased susceptibility to infections due to chronic illness
options.D: Immediate lifelong immunity acquired from farm work

explanation: Chronic illnesses like diabetes can slow down healing and weaken the immune response, meaning this patient catches infections much more easily. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h6)

question: Which of these nursing actions is a clear example of primary prevention focused on the host?

options.A: Screening blood samples for early signs of malaria
options.B: Providing physical therapy after a stroke
options.C: Treating severe complications in an intensive care unit

explanation: Primary prevention stops disease before it even starts. Giving vaccines helps the body build a strong defense way ahead of any exposure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of secondary prevention strategies for a patient?

options.A: Preventing any future contact between the host and the environment
options.B: Rehabilitating a patient after permanent disability has occurred
options.C: Eliminating the vector species completely from a tropical region
options.D: Detecting and treating an infection early before it causes severe illness

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about catching things early! Think of screenings and prompt treatments that stop a small infection from turning into a major emergency. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T79#GNS214_U1_T79_h7)
